catalog_quote: Rendille clearly makes use of pitch as a prosodic feature. ... In applying these criteria to Rendille, one would interpret the high pitch as stress, not tone. In Rendille one finds monosyllabic words, albeit few, which are only distinguished by a difference in pitch ... Looking at the question diachronically, one may say that present-day Rendille, which at first analysis appears to be a tone language, developed out of a bound stress language, i.e. word stress was bound to the penultimate or antepenultimate, depending on syllable weight. Everything considered it may be best to say, on the lines of McCawley (1968:135), that Rendille is a pitch-accent language. Pitch in Rendille expresses merely a location, like in Japanese, and not features of individual syllables as in a real tone language such as Chinese. If, in Rendille, the high-pitched mora is located, the pitch of the other moras is…
sweep_summary: Rendille (rend1243) is in the catalog as 'tonal' (TONAL-OR-PITCH-ACCENT) on Oomen 1981 (pitch-accent: one H mora per word, masculine penultimate mora vs feminine final mora) with Sim 1981 and Mous 2021 as support. The sweep's four stress-titled items are really two works by Steve (Owen Stephen) Pillinger: the 1988 paper 'Tone and accent in Rendille: a preliminary investigation' (Cushitic-Omotic, Buske, pp. 503-511; Glottolog 43658; Glottolog 671785 is the same paper mis-attributed to the volume editors Bechhaus-Gerst and Serzisko) and the 1989 SOAS PhD 'Accent, tone and prosodic structure in Rendille, with particular reference to the nominal system' (323 pp.; Glottolog 46034 and duplicate 684506). Both are squarely about accent/tone placement in Rendille and are the best primary treatments, but neither could be obtained: no DOI (the DOI Mous 2021 attaches to Pillinger 1988, 10.15460/aethiopica.12.1.127, resolves to an unrelated Voigt book review in Aethiopica 12 — a mis-assignment, now recorded); eprints.soas.ac.uk does not resolve; SOAS worktribe, EThOS (now back online), HathiTrust and Google Books search-inside are Cloudflare/anti-bot blocked; OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, CORE and Google Books API returned 429; SIL record 9962 says 'Not Available Online'; archive.org holds only the 1996 Berlin proceedings (different volume). What is known of them is second-hand via Mous 2021 (already in the catalog): underlyingly accentual, tonal at the surface (H spreading, contour simplification, downstep); some nominative/genitive nouns with no H; concessive verbs H-HL (Pillinger 1989: 236); Rendille 'developed from tone to accent'. Nothing read in this sweep contradicts or supersedes the catalog coding; Pillinger 1989 remains the high-priority acquisition (SOAS library / British Library EThOS order / ProQuest). Receipts and search records are in and.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: all segments of the deciding quotation, the domain quote and the exceptions quote are verbatim in the held archive.org scanned of Afroasiatic Linguistics 8(1) at the stated sections/pages (Oomen §2.3 pp.38-39, §3.1.1-3.1.2 pp.40-41; Sim §2.3 p.4), and the Mous 2021 secondary quotes are verbatim in the held SPiL Plus 62 PDF text. (2) Deciding source: a 1981 primary fieldwork article on nominal morphology with an explicit, argued accentual analysis ('pitch-accent language', one H mora per word, gender-indexed locus, mora-counting), corroborated by Sim 1981 ('Rendille is tonal'), Hartell 1993 (screen), Heine 1978 (fetched sources now: Sam/Rendille data transcribed with H/HL/L tones + accent, gender by H-L vs L-H contour) and by Mous 2021's specialist survey relaying Pillinger 1988/1989 (accent underlyingly, surface tone rules incl. downstep, accentless noun case forms) and Esser 1991.

sources.quote: 'A systematic comparative treatment of tone and accent in the Sam languages has not yet been attempted... (1) It is likely that Proto-Sam was a tone language distinguishing between High, Low and High-falling tone... One of the functions of tone was to distinguish sex gender of nouns... *ínam M boy : *inám F girl... the tone pattern is High-Low with Masculine and Low-High with Feminine nouns... (3) In addition to three tones, Proto-Sam can be assumed to have marked an accent which in most, though not all, cases coincides with High tone.
